newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Acesita sees improved second half.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Acesita sees improved second half.

text.p: Brazilian private specialty steelmaker Acesita said it expects to improve its performance in the second half, with sales growing 15 percent in the period as the economy heats up by year-end.
Acesita, which posted a 29.4 million real loss in the first half, said a drop in international steel prices and lower consumption in the domestic market led to the firm's poor results.

"Our sales dropped to 299,000 from 330,000 tonnes of steel in the first half because demand fell amid an economic slowdown," said a company spokesman, responding to criticism that Acesita's gloomy performance, reflected in the company's stock price, was less related to market factors.

Gazeta Mercantil newspaper said on Wednesday analysts attributed a nearly 60 percent plunge in Acesita's preferred shares since the beginning of 1996 partly to the firm's strategy to expand and diversify.

The paper said analysts feel Acesita President Wilson Brumer erred in deciding earlier this year to make an 850 million real offer to buy stakes in three other steel mills -- Usiminas USI.SA, Cosipa and Cia. Siderurgica de Tubarao (CST).
Acesita, South America's only stainless steel producer, ended up buying only a stake in steel slab maker CST for 504 million reais.
The spokesman justified the decision to diversify by saying that the company moved to reduce its dependence on stainless steel.
But he noted Acesita's core business continues to be stainless steel output, which currently accounts for 25 percent of the firm's total production and 55 percent of its annual revenues.
Evidence of Acesita's commitment to the production of stainless steel is the company's ongoing investment plan, said the spokesman.

Acesita has invested $344 million since 1994 in part to expand its stainless steel output to 290,000 from 160,000 tonnes at the end of next year, he said. With the expansion, stainless steel will account for 40 percent of the company's production and 70 percent of its annual revenues.
The Acesita spokesman also said the company hopes to restore investor trust in the stock. He noted long-term investors have not sold their shares.
"We have the impression that long-term investors understood better the deal (regarding the purchase of stakes in other steel mills)," he said.
